title: VPC Policy Evolution — Postmortem & Runbook Draft
content:
Summary:

On 2026-07-12 02:17 UTC we observed a progressive loss of control-plane reachability for a subset (~7%) of Private deployments after an automated VPC policy sync change rolled out. Affected customers reported increased 502/504 and failed healthchecks against the control plane; platform-level metrics showed elevated control-plane HA re-election and connection resets. Impact lasted ~1h10m for the worst-off tenants; full mitigation and rollback were completed by 03:30 UTC.

This doc is a postmortem of the event and a draft of a runbook/playbook for handling similar VPC policy evolution incidents in the future. It contains timeline, root cause analysis, immediate mitigations used, suggested runbook steps (with commands to run during triage), and action items.

Incident timeline (UTC):
- 02:00 — Scheduled policy sync cron started for edge-vpc-policy-updates (batch size 50).
- 02:12 — First customer alert: customer-monitoring reported control-plane heartbeat misses (Customer X). Pager triggered to oncall SRE.
- 02:15 — We started seeing a spike in error-rate for control-plane gRPC connections in region-us-west-2; telemetry indicated many TCP RSTs from customer VPC egress points.
- 02:20 — Narrowed to subset of customers using policy-template v3.2 where iptables translation for SNAT had an ordering change.
- 02:28 — Oncall attempted automated rollback of policy sync (reverted CRs via infra pipeline) — rollback failed for ~10% of targets due to partial delivery and an unsupported combined patch path.
- 02:35 — Mitigation: temporarily enabled fallback route policy to force control-plane traffic through alternate peering link (bypassed iptables SNAT path) — reduced error-rate by ~60%.
- 03:00 — Completed manual remediation for highest impact customers (3 customers) by applying emergency ACL exception.
- 03:21 — Infra team completed full rollback for remaining customers.
- 03:30 — Metrics normalized, ongoing verification and post-incident monitoring extended for 24h.

Impact:
- Approx 7% of private deployments experienced control-plane connectivity degradation (timeouts, occasional API errors).
- No customer data corruption reported. Some webhooks/retries were delayed.
- SLA blips for 4 enterprise customers; CS and account teams notified.

Immediate root cause (summary):
- The automated policy sync introduced an iptables translation rule reordering in policy-template v3.2. The new rule ordering caused SNAT to be applied prior to connection tracking normalization in some on-prem appliance versions used by customers. The result: established connections to the control plane saw asymmetric pathing and unexpected source IPs, which triggered ingress firewall rules on the control plane side to reject traffic or reset connections.

Contributing factors:
1) Policy sync batch logic applied template changes in large batches (size 50) without a small canary cohort for new template semantics.
2) No dried-run validation against customer-managed firewall fingerprinting behavior (many customers have appliances that do strict reverse-path or anti-Spoof checks).
3) Rollback mechanism did not support the particular three-way patch sequence we generated; partial rollbacks were left in an inconsistent state.
4) Alerts were tied to control-plane error-rate but not to early signs like TCP RST spikes or SNAT/IP change events in flow logs.
5) Oncall runbook lacked a clear step for toggling the alternate peering path that bypasses the SNAT reorder.

Detailed technical root cause (short):
- template v3.2 changed NAT rule ordering in the iptables-save output produced by our templating engine. Customer on-prem NAT/inspection appliances from vendor Z (versions 4.8–5.1) are sensitive to source-IP changes mid-connection because they track flows by tuple including source. When SNAT applied in the new order, the apparent source switched before the appliance finished inspection, leading the appliance to drop/RESET packets. This produced TCP RST from the customer side, causing gRPC streams to fail.

How we detected it:
- Customer alerts -> cross-referenced with platform telemetry (gRPC errors, connection resets) -> inspected flow logs (VPC flow logs showed sudden SNATed source addresses) -> correlated to policy sync timeline from infra pipeline logs.

Mitigations performed during the incident (with commands used):
- Emergency fallback: enabled alternate peering path (peer-bypass) to avoid SNAT translation sequence.
  - CLI (infractl): infractl peering enable-bypass --peer-id peer-us-west-2-alt --target-ids <affected-tenant-ids>
- Manual per-tenant exception: patching VPC policy to add transient allow-rule for control-plane CIDR before SNAT rules to prevent firewall from dropping connections.
  - Example patch (kubectl style pseudo-CR):
    kubectl patch vpcpolicy <tenant-policy> --type=json -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/rules/0","value":{"action":"allow","cidr":"34.56.78.0/24","priority":10}}]'
- Rollback attempt via infra pipeline (failed partial):
  - infra-pipeline revert --change-id pr-1023 --batch-size 50
- Final manual rollback for remaining targets via infractl: infractl policy apply --file policy-v3.1.json --target <id>

Post-incident diagnosis steps we ran (for root cause verification):
- Collected VPC flow logs from affected tenants and compared src/dst addresses before/after change.
- Captured tcpdump on control-plane frontends to observe RSTs and confirm on-prem devices were issuing resets.
- Replayed iptables-save output from templates and diffed v3.1 vs v3.2 ordering.
- Engaged vendor Z to confirm device behavior on SNAT ordering.

Proposed runbook (draft) — immediate actions for oncall when seeing similar symptoms:
1) Triage: confirm scope and severity. Check:
   - Control-plane 5xx/gRPC error increase (alerts).
   - VPC flow logs: look for sudden source IP changes or SNAT patterns.
   - TCP-level: check for RST bursts to control-plane ports.
   - Infra pipeline activity: any policy/template changes pushed in last 30m.
2) Contain:
   - If a policy/template change is in-flight, pause the pipeline for subsequent batches: infra-pipeline pause --job <job-id>
   - Enable peer-bypass route for affected region(s) (infractl peering enable-bypass --peer-id <id> --targets <ids>)
   - If peer-bypass not available, add a high-priority transient allow-rule for control-plane CIDR to the tenant policy (kubectl patch or infractl policy apply)
3) Mitigate:
   - For customers with appliances known to be sensitive (vendor Z list maintained in confluence), escalate to manual remediation and coordinate CS for customer communication.
4) Rollback:
   - Use infractl policy apply --file policy-v3.1.json --target <id> for manual rollback if automated revert fails.
5) Verify:
   - Confirm gRPC success rate recovery, absence of RSTs in tcpdump, and stable flow logs for 15–30m.
6) Post-incident:
   - Capture full packet captures and flow logs; open a vendor support request if appliances are implicated.

Runbook quick-check checklist (one-line steps):
- Confirm pipeline job id and batch size.
- Pause infra pipeline.
- Toggle peer-bypass for affected region.
- Apply transient allow-rule if peer-bypass unavailable.
- Escalate to infra lead if rollback fails for >10% targets.

Testing and prevention plan (recommended):
1) Canary changes: shrink batch-size to 5 for first deploy of any template that touches NAT order; require 2 successful canary customers with different appliance vendors (Z and Y) before scaling.
2) Dry-run verification: add step to pipeline that runs iptables-save emulation and calls a fingerprinting harness that simulates vendor appliance behavior (repo: infra/sim/firewall-fingerprint).
3) Expand telemetry: add flow-log-derived metrics for SNAT-change rate and TCP RST rate per-tenant; create alert if either spikes after policy changes.
4) Rollback hardening: ensure infra-pipeline supports three-way patch reversal for template upgrades (owner: infra-engineering).
5) Maintain a curated list of customer appliance families and known sensitivities (Confluence page) and flag them during template planning.
6) Peer-bypass coverage: expand alternate peering routes to all regions as a documented escape hatch and automate a safe toggle via infractl.

Action items (owners):
- Infra: implement small-canary default for template changes + pipeline toggle (owner: Diego Alvarez) — due 2026-08-02.
- Observability: add SNAT-change and tcp-rst per-tenant metrics + Pager rule (owner: Samir Rao) — due 2026-07-28.
- Infra: harden rollback semantics to support three-way patch sequences (owner: Marta Liu) — due 2026-08-09.
- Security/Policy: draft pre-deploy checklist including customer appliance sensitivity lookup (owner: Priya Kapoor) — due 2026-07-22.
- SRE: finalize runbook and add to oncall handbook (owner: Aisha Patel) — due 2026-07-19.

Communication notes (to be used by CS/GTM):
- Draft message template: brief explanation that a policy template upgrade temporarily changed NAT ordering which some on-prem devices treat as a connection teardown; rollback and mitigations are in place and we are expanding testing to avoid recurrence.
- Notification: reach out to all affected accounts with timeline + temporary mitigation applied and offer a follow-up call.

Appendix — Useful diagnostics and commands:
- Check active infra pipeline jobs: infra-pipeline list --filter policy-sync --active
- Pause pipeline job: infra-pipeline pause --job <job-id>
- View recent template changes: infractl templates history --name policy-template --limit 50
- Enable peer-bypass (safe toggle): infractl peering enable-bypass --peer-id <peer-id> --targets <tenant-ids>
- Apply policy file manually: infractl policy apply --file policy-v3.1.json --target <tenant-id>
- Get VPC flow logs (example BigQuery export query pattern): SELECT * FROM vpc_flow_logs WHERE tenant_id IN (<ids>) AND timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 1 HOUR) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP();
- Tcpdump on control-plane frontend: sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 host <customer-egress-ip> and port 443 -w /tmp/cp-<tenant>-20260712.pcap

Notes to self / open questions (for follow-up):
- Confirm whether any other template changes in pipeline could cause similar reordering in other iptables sections (mangle, nat prerouting).
- Vendor Z has acknowledged the behavior as expected on some firmware; get specific firmware matrix.
- Evaluate the option of template-level annotation that marks 'SNAT-ordering-sensitive' so our pipeline auto-reduces batch size.

Status: draft — please review and add corrections/edge cases I missed. Once we agree on the runbook, I'll add it to the SRE oncall handbook and schedule a tabletop for the infra + vendor + SRE + CS group.

Last reviewed by: Marta Liu (2026-07-13)
